passages.text: Training large language models (LLMs) entails a fundamental trade-off: memory-efficient optimizers such as Adam discard cross-parameter curvature, whereas full-curvature methods such as SOAP can accelerate convergence at prohibitive memory costs. We introduce Clean , a memory-efficient and full-curvature optimizer designed to resolve this bottleneck. Clean leverages the randomized Nyström method to accurately approximate the left and right preconditioners in SOAP, and to reduce the optimizer’s memory complexity from quadratic to linear in terms of model dimensions. We subsequently reintegrate the off-subspace components to capture curvature information beyond the low-rank approximation, preserving rich curvature at minimal memory cost. We further propose Q-Clean , a low-precision variant that aggressively compresses optimizer states. Q-Clean reduces optimizer memory consumption by over 50% compared to Muon when pre-training a LLaMA-1.3B architecture, all while maintaining strong and competitive predictive performance. Notably, Clean operates with a smaller optimizer-state footprint than standard AdamW while reaching AdamW’s final performance 26% faster in wall-clock time. passages.text: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

passages.section: Low-rank bias and the limits of norm descriptions.
passages.text: Gunasekar et al. (2017) investigate implicit regularization in two-layer matrix factorization and conjecture a nuclear-norm characterization in a restricted commuting setting. Arora et al. (2019) extend the analysis to depth and derive singular-value-dependent mobility under balanced gradient flow, showing that depth strengthens the tendency toward low-rank solutions. Razin and Cohen (2020) construct matrix-completion problems in which norms diverge as the loss vanishes, demonstrating the limits of a universal norm-minimization account. Li et al. (2021) instead develop a greedy low-rank learning interpretation under explicit assumptions. A complementary trajectory perspective is provided by Neural Tangent Kernel and lazy-training analyses, which characterize sufficiently wide networks through a linearization around initialization and an approximately fixed kernel governing function-space evolution ( Jacot et al., 2018 ; Lee et al., 2019 ; Sabanayagam et al., 2022 ) . In contrast, our analysis retains the nonlinear multiplicative parameterization and its evolving, optimizer-dependent spectral mobility, allowing us to compare the birth, saturation, and decay of singular modes before convergence.

passages.section: Implicit bias of Adam and related adaptive methods.
passages.text: Cattaneo et al. (2023) use backward error analysis to characterize corrections to Adam and RMSProp dynamics, relating implicit regularization to hyperparameters and training stage. The classification literature builds on the maximum margin characterization of GD for separable data ( Soudry et al., 2018 ) . Wang et al. (2021) study limiting parameter directions in homogeneous classification under their adaptive flow assumptions. Zhang et al. (2024) establish a maximum ℓ ∞ \ell_{\infty} margin result for full batch Adam in separable linear classification. Xie and Li (2024) connect AdamW, which includes decoupled weight decay, to ℓ ∞ \ell_{\infty} -norm constrained optimization under full-batch assumptions. Vasudeva et al. (2026) analyze a difference in feature learning between Adam and GD in a Gaussian classification model with two layer ReLU networks. These results concern distinct losses, optimizer conventions, or notions of bias. Our squared loss analysis studies finite singular amplitudes and phase times without weight decay, so classification margin results do not directly determine its birth or saturation laws.

We next consider a less structured setting in which the effective predictor is trained by underdetermined linear regression as described in App. F . This experiment tests whether the qualitative predictions persist once our simplifying assumptions Assumptions 1 , 2 and 3 are removed. Fig. 16 shows that the optimizers reach comparable training losses and converge to nearly identical final singular spectra. This agreement is important: the pronounced differences observed during training are not simply consequences of one method converging to a substantially different level of fit. Nevertheless, the stable and effective ranks evolve differently. Thus similar terminal predictors need not imply similar spectral learning dynamics. We train the same deep linear predictor on an underdetermined, nonwhitened regression problem using GD, Adam, Muon, cumulative Shampoo, and KFAC. All methods reach comparable final loss and final spectra of W W despite substantially different transient dynamics shown by the stable rank and effective rank throughout training. The optimizer geometry strongly changes how quickly spectral mass concentrates.

The singular value trajectories in Fig. 17 make this distinction particularly clear. GD exhibits pronounced separation between the emergence times of successive singular values, consistent with the factorization induced small mode barrier derived in the aligned setting. Adam substantially compresses these delays. Muon produces a markedly more synchronized growth of the singular spectrum, consistent with normalization reducing mode dependent mobility differences. Cumulative Shampoo also accelerates weaker spectral components after its preconditioner has accumulated sufficient history, while K-FAC produces comparatively smooth growth across the spectrum through curvature correction. These effects remain visible even though the singular vectors are not fixed and the data covariance couples the modes. The experiment therefore supports the interpretation of the theoretical phase laws as mechanisms governing transient spectral learning rather than merely properties of the special aligned model. Exact exponents depend on the aligned reduction, but the resulting qualitative distinctions persist in the more practical underdetermined regression problem. Although all methods approach similar final singular spectra, their transient spectrum differ substantially. The qualitative optimizer dependent dynamics predicted by the aligned phase analysis remain visible even when the empirical data covariance couples singular directions and the exact scalar mode reduction no longer holds.

passages.text: Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter’s rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. On DeiT-Tiny, risk is lowest at rank one and rises sharply as the adapter becomes able to fit the noisy labels, forming an interpolation cliff. Past the peak, risk falls again, but every tested post-peak rank that still saves parameters remains above dense risk. Rank-one LoRA outperforms dense fine-tuning on three of the four vision backbones, consistent with strong regularization at small rank. LoRA thus exhibits a second descent, but matches dense risk only after losing its parameter advantage, first on DeiT-Tiny at four times dense’s projection weights. Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter’s rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. On DeiT-Tiny, risk is lowest at rank one and rises sharply as the adapter becomes able to fit the noisy labels, forming an interpolation cliff. Past the peak, risk falls again, but every tested post-peak rank that still saves parameters remains above dense risk. LoRA thus exhibits a second descent, but matches dense risk only after losing its parameter advantage, first on DeiT-Tiny at four times dense’s projection weights. Our optimizer extends recent matrix optimizers for full-parameter training to the manifold of fixed-rank matrices by interpreting them as normalization under a rotated basis. We show how rotation and normalization can be integrated with the fixed-rank manifold efficiently. Our optimizer converges faster to lower held-out loss and achieves better or comparable downstream performance on both supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks.

Large language models (LLMs) based on the transformer architecture ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) have achieved remarkable success in recent years ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Touvron et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . These models typically adopt a pretraining-finetuning paradigm, where large-scale pretraining equips a model with general capabilities and subsequent finetuning adapts it to specific downstream applications. However, as LLMs grow to billions of parameters, full-parameter finetuning becomes expensive in both computation and memory. Such a challenge has motivated the development of parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , which only update a small fraction of all parameters. Among these approaches, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) has emerged as a particularly effective method and has been widely adopted. LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and parametrizes the weight updates as products of low-rank matrices, substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters and the memory footprint, while maintaining competitive performance. Compared with full-parameter training, LoRA exhibits a unique geometric structure induced by its low-rank factorization. Specifically, the low-rank matrices have infinitely many reparameterizations that represent the same weight update, since the model’s output depends on these low-rank factors only through their product. This invariance, commonly referred to as gauge symmetry, suggests that optimization should respect the underlying geometry of the weight space of the LoRA parametrization. Motivated by this observation, we revisit the optimization of LoRA and aim to explicitly incorporate its gauge symmetry into the design of the optimization algorithm.

We design our optimizer on the manifold of fixed-rank matrices, aiming to optimize the product of the low-rank factors directly rather than each factor separately. We extend the recent advances in matrix optimizers ( Gong et al., 2026 ; Jordan et al., 2024 ; Vyas et al., 2025 ) to the fixed-rank manifold by interpreting their update rules as normalization under a rotated basis. Our optimizer applies row and column normalization in a conditioning frame defined by the left singular vectors of the tangent momentum, projects the resulting direction back onto the tangent space, and retracts to the fixed-rank manifold. By exploiting the low-rank structure of tangent vectors, all operations can be performed using thin factors without materializing full weight-sized matrices. We refer to our proposed optimizer as RoM ( Ro tated M anifold Optimization). We evaluate RoM on supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks. RoM achieves substantially lower held-out loss and better or comparable downstream task performance compared with other LoRA optimizers, with only modest additional computational overhead.

We evaluate RoM on supervised finetuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) tasks, comparing its optimization and downstream performance against existing LoRA optimizers. We describe the experimental setup in Section 4.1 , present the SFT and RL results in Section 4.2 and 4.3 , respectively, and further study the contribution of its components and its sensitivity to learning-rate selection in Section 4.4 . passages.text: While Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) enables efficient task specialization, its learned updates can compromise capabilities beyond the target task. We identify adaptation imbalance : a few singular directions dominate the trained update, leaving its performance sensitive to how gains are allocated. We argue that learning where to adapt does not ensure that adaptation gains are well balanced . This motivates LoRA-Norm , a post-training normalization method that retains learned directions while rebalancing their gains. LoRA-Norm combines spectral rebalancing, a fixed nonlinear transformation of singular values, with nuclear-norm restoration, which preserves the original total spectral mass. It requires no calibration data or additional training and introduces no inference overhead. Across two backbones and three adaptation tasks, LoRA-Norm improves average specialization and capability retention, outperforming the evaluated post-hoc spectral pruning and gradient-guided editing configurations on both measures. Stronger functional equalization brings no consistent additional gains, revealing that balancing adapter gains and equalizing their responses are distinct objectives.

Our central argument is that learning where to adapt does not ensure that adaptation gains are well balanced . Training jointly determines directions and gains through a source-task objective, but the resulting configuration can remain improvable for specialization and broader capability retention. Prior work establishes the feasibility of post-training refinement through weight interpolation ( Wortsman et al., 2022 ) , spectral pruning ( Kumaravelu et al., 2026 ) , and calibration-gradient-guided reweighting ( Tian et al., 2026 ) . We investigate a simpler intervention: a fixed normalization rule that revisits the gains of a completed adapter using only its parameters. Figure 1: Learn the directions, normalize the gains. LoRA training learns useful adaptation directions, but the gains assigned to these directions can become imbalanced. LoRA-Norm keeps the learned directions fixed and rebalances only their gains after training, improving specialization while preserving capabilities beyond the target task. We propose LoRA-Norm , which combines spectral rebalancing with nuclear-norm restoration , as shown in Fig. 1 . Spectral rebalancing applies a short, fixed sequence of nonlinear transformations to the singular values while preserving their associated directions. Nuclear-norm restoration rescales the transformed gains to preserve their original sum within each module. This changes the allocation of spectral mass without requiring an exactly flat spectrum. The edited update is reconstructed as standard low-rank factors with the original adapter configuration and scaling. LoRA-Norm therefore requires no calibration data or additional training and introduces no inference overhead.

We evaluate 18 trained adapters spanning two backbones and three adaptation tasks in coding, mathematical reasoning, and instruction following. LoRA-Norm improves average target-task performance and capability retention, exceeding the evaluated spectral-pruning and gradient-guided editing configurations on both measures. These results show that the same learned directions can support better deployment performance after gain normalization, without any additional training. Our analysis also clarifies what this improvement means. Preserving nuclear norm does not preserve update magnitude, and a direction’s functional contribution depends on both its gain and the inputs that activate it ( Paischer et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) . Controls matched to LoRA-Norm’s activation-weighted update energy recover much of its benefit, while stronger functional equalization provides no consistent additional gains. Thus, balancing adapter gains and equalizing their responses are distinct objectives . Directional concentration is useful for characterizing an adapter, but uniformity alone is insufficient to judge whether an edit improves specialization and retention. In a nutshell, our contributions are summarized as follows: • Empirical insight. We characterize adaptation imbalance in trained LoRA adapters and show that their learned directions can support improved specialization and capability retention through post-training gain adjustment. • Practical method. We introduce LoRA-Norm, a fixed spectral normalization procedure that preserves learned directions and per-module nuclear mass, requiring neither calibration data nor additional training or inference operations.

• Functional analysis. We examine gain redistribution alongside update strength through matched-strength controls and activation-aware interventions, showing why stronger response equalization is not a reliable objective for adapter refinement.

WiSE-FT interpolates pretrained and fine-tuned weights to improve robustness ( Wortsman et al., 2022 ) , corresponding to scaling a LoRA update. Spectral Unforgetting applies hard singular-value thresholding through DG-Hard ( Abro and Tahir, 2026 ) ; SLoRA filters updates by subspace similarity to the base model ( Yang et al., 2026 ) ; and PARA uses a global singular-value threshold for nonuniform rank compression ( Kumaravelu et al., 2026 ) . Safety-oriented methods include S3LoRA, which uses spectral sharpness to guide post-hoc pruning ( Ao and Rumchurn, 2025 ) , and CSULoRA, which smoothly attenuates update components relative to an estimated safety-aligned subspace ( Marchenko Breneur et al., 2026 ) . Spectral Surgery uses calibration gradients to reweight gains while fixing singular directions, with nuclear-mass restoration ( Tian et al., 2026 ) . LoRA-Norm builds on this fixed-direction formulation, replacing gradient-guided reweighting with a fixed data-free map and studying capability retention and matched-strength controls. LoRA-Norm applies a finite nonlinear transformation with per-module nuclear-norm restoration. Scalar and exact-flattening controls test the roles of update strength and spectral shape.

Our results show that the same learned adaptation directions can support better specialization and capability retention after gain adjustment. LoRA-Norm revisits this allocation through fixed spectral rebalancing and per-module nuclear-norm restoration, without calibration data, retraining, or inference overhead. Across 18 adapters spanning two backbones and three tasks, it improves both objectives on average. Energy-matched controls recover much of the benefit, while stronger functional equalization yields no consistent further gains, limiting claims of an independent spectral-shape advantage. Thus, balancing adapter gains and equalizing functional responses are distinct objectives. Broader model and task coverage and further controlled replications would help assess generality.

Fira ( Chen et al., 2024 ) pursues this goal by combining adaptive optimization of low-rank projected gradients with scaled residual updates. Its projection bases are obtained through SVD and reused across multiple optimization steps to amortize decomposition costs. However, as the leading gradient subspace drifts during training, reused bases may become less aligned with important directions of subsequent gradients, potentially limiting the effectiveness of adaptive optimization, while more frequent basis refreshes incur additional computational costs. LoRA-GA ( Wang et al., 2024 ) uses full-gradient information to initialize the factors so that their initial induced weight-space gradient better approximates that of full fine-tuning. Both branches use quantities computed from the same pre-update parameters. The normal branch introduces no additional momentum or variance buffers for the base weights. passages.text: One might think that learning the identity function with a deep linear residual network is trivial – the path along residual connections already implements the identity, and so the network need only drive its weights to zero. However, this zero-weight solution is just one point on an entire manifold of population-loss minimizers, each corresponding to a different decomposition of the identity across the network’s layers. Although the population loss does not distinguish among these solutions, stochastic gradient descent (SGD) reproducibly favors particular ones. For instance, under anisotropic label noise, the learned layers exhibit a noise-dependent spectrum; even with weight decay, SGD does not generally recover the zero-weight solution. Changing only the parametrization, while leaving the set of realizable functions unchanged, yields different behavior: factoring each weight matrix as a product of two matrices causes the weights to collapse to zero, even without explicit weight decay.

While perhaps mysterious and unintuitive at first, these phenomena can be understood through the lens of entropic loss , which augments the population loss with a term proportional to the expected squared norm of the minibatch gradient ( Ziyin et al., 2025 ) . On the identity manifold, the population loss is constant, while the entropic term distinguishes among these decompositions. We characterize its minimizers analytically and use them to derive predictions for the structure of solutions favored by SGD. Under isotropic label noise, these minimizers are orthogonal factorizations; under anisotropic noise, the first layer’s singular values are the fourth roots of the eigenvalues of the noise covariance, and weight decay compresses this spectrum toward one without recovering the zero-weight solution. In deeper networks, this noise-dependent spectral structure is confined to the first and last layers. Under the factored parametrization, the entropic term is minimized only at the zero-weight solution. Networks trained with SGD closely match these predictions. passages.text: What makes great scientists great? Even as AI systems start to make progress on open problems, scientists remain far ahead of them at sensing which prior idea, buried in an ever-growing archive of research, a new problem needs. To study this skill, we draw on researchers who know firsthand which earlier work advanced their completed projects, with papers serving as pointers to the ideas within. Using our automated pipeline that makes author annotation scalable, we build ScholarCatalyst by having 184 lead authors of 207 recent computer science papers label which candidates did or could have advanced their project, each with a detailed rationale. We introduce a retrieval task with author-provided judgments: given an initial research question, retrieve these papers from only the literature available when the project began. Agentic search does no better than embedding retrieval (0.42 vs. 0.48 Recall@20) despite calling that same retriever as a tool. Even an agent built on Claude Fable 5.1, which may have seen the completed papers during training, reaches only 0.51 R@20. These results highlight the need for new training recipes that equip models with expert intuition for searching broad corpora. We envision ScholarCatalyst as a step toward scientific agents that can take a half-formed idea and point to the prior research it needs.

All systems struggle to retrieve catalyst papers. Current retrievers miss most of the papers that inspired a project ( Table 3 ). General-purpose dense retrievers perform best, yet place 39% of author-identified inspiration papers in the top 20 for CoreQ and 51% for SubQ . Scientific-document retrievers (SPECTER2, OpenScholar) trail the general-purpose models by at least 16 points on CoreQ and 27 points on SubQ at Recall@20. BM25 and LateOn trail by 15–16 points on CoreQ and 18–25 points on SubQ . Together, these results suggest that domain-specific training on citation signals does not by itself solve this task. Among the pre-cutoff systems in our main experiment, CoreQ is harder than SubQ , consistent with its longer queries and smaller, almost entirely cited positive sets ( Table 2 ). We show later that reranking with an oracle candidate pool recovers part of this gap ( Section 4.4 ). Agentic search does not improve over embedding retrieval. We compare LLM search agents built on pre-cutoff models (GPT-4.1 and o3) against the strongest embedding model ( Table 3 ). Grep-based search, despite its recent success as a lightweight alternative to embedding retrieval ( Li et al., 2026 ; Sen et al., 2026 ) , performs substantially worse. It finds only 8% of gold query–paper pairs during search, compared with 46% for the tool-calling agent ( Figure 6 ).

We attribute this gap to candidate coverage , since regardless of how a model reasons, an agent can interact with the corpus only through its search queries. As the corpus scales, this constraint becomes more important because an agent can inspect only a small fraction of the corpus. Consistent with this account, agent recall rises with backbone capability yet remains close to the embedding retriever’s even for the strongest model ( Figure 6 ). If coverage is the limiting factor, progress will require embedding retrievers that surface inspiration papers in the first place and agents that build on those results to guide further exploration. We report Fable 5.1 separately because it falls outside our knowledge cutoff, and we analyze its results, together with agent failure cases and retrieval rationales, in Sections D.3 and D.6 .

passages.text: Stronger rerankers benefit more from better candidate coverage. To separate retrieval coverage from recognition performance, we apply LLM-based reranking to the top- K K candidates from Gemini-Embedding-2 on a randomly sampled subset of 50 CoreQ and 50 SubQ queries. We compare reranking with and without gold injection, which replaces negative candidates with positive papers missing from the set while keeping the pool size fixed. Stronger rerankers gain more in Recall@5 from gold injection ( Figure 6 ). The growing gap suggests that candidate coverage limits how much we can benefit from stronger rerankers: their ability to select useful papers matters only when those papers enter the pool. Better retrieval could therefore yield larger gains as rerankers improve. Reranking prompts and procedures are provided in Section D.2 .

We introduce Clean , a memory-efficient and full-curvature optimizer designed to resolve this bottleneck. Clean leverages the randomized Nyström method to accurately approximate the left and right preconditioners in SOAP, and to reduce the optimizer’s memory complexity from quadratic to linear in terms of model dimensions. We subsequently reintegrate the off-subspace components to capture curvature information beyond the low-rank approximation, preserving rich curvature at minimal memory cost. We further propose Q-Clean , a low-precision variant that aggressively compresses optimizer states. Q-Clean reduces optimizer memory consumption by over 50% compared to Muon when pre-training a LLaMA-1.3B architecture, all while maintaining strong and competitive predictive performance. Notably, Clean operates with a smaller optimizer-state footprint than standard AdamW while reaching AdamW’s final performance 26% faster in wall-clock time. Furthermore, our methods uniquely enable the pre-training of a 13B-parameter model on a single 80GB GPU, providing a scalable, efficient, and accessible approach to large-scale model optimization. $*$ $*$ footnotetext: Equal contribution.

decision.reason: Selected seven papers covering the profile’s strongest distinct priorities: weight spectra, low-rank compression, LoRA optimization and label noise, memory-efficient pretraining, and research-paper retrieval. Reviewer disagreements were resolved by fit to those priorities, not by vote: continual-learning LoRA papers, the restricted Newton–Schulz guarantee, general context compression, and compression without low-rank factorization lost out to more direct candidates. selections.summary: Analyzes how GD, Adam-like, Muon, Shampoo, and K-FAC update geometry changes singular-mode birth, decay, and effective-rank trajectories in matrix factorization. Its broader regression experiment finds different transient spectra despite similar final fits.
selections.relevance: Directly addresses how optimization shapes weight spectra and low-rank bias, while remaining a model-based rather than LLM-scale result.

evidence.quote: Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC.
All methods reach comparable final loss and final spectra of W W despite substantially different transient dynamics shown by the stable rank and effective rank throughout training.

selections.summary: Learns low-rank projection subspaces jointly against model-output KL while keeping pretrained weights frozen. At 70% compression on Llama-2-7B, it reports WikiText-2 perplexity of 10.9 versus 13.3 for the strongest baseline.
selections.relevance: Tests preservation of LLM quality under low-rank weight factorization. It is post-training compression, not evidence that pretraining itself improves compressibility.

evidence.quote: All projectors are optimized jointly against a global objective—the KL divergence to the dense model’s output distribution or the model’s original training loss—while the pretrained weights remain frozen.
At − 70 % -70\% compression, LSP brings Llama-2-7B to 10.9 10.9 WikiText-2 perplexity and 42.2 % 42.2\% mean zero-shot accuracy, versus 13.3 13.3 and 36.0 % 36.0\% for the strongest baseline.

selections.summary: Uses module-matched, paired-seed LoRA rank sweeps under label noise. In its Qwen2.5-7B classification experiment, every sampled rank, including parameter parity, has higher test NLL than dense fine-tuning of the same modules.
selections.relevance: Combines LoRA rank, practical language-model fine-tuning, and generalization under noisy labels.

evidence.quote: We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed.
Every sampled rank, parity included, remains behind dense in all three seeds, while the valley reference reads Rec > 1 \mathrm{Rec}>1 at every sampled rank from r = 448 r{=}448 on.

selections.summary: Proposes a fixed-rank-manifold LoRA optimizer that accounts for factorization gauge symmetry. Reported supervised fine-tuning results show lower validation loss, while some downstream accuracy differences are small relative to seed variation.
selections.relevance: Directly addresses optimization geometry and practical language-model behavior of low-rank updates.

evidence.quote: Our optimizer applies row and column normalization in a conditioning frame defined by the left singular vectors of the tangent momentum, projects the resulting direction back onto the tangent space, and retracts to the fixed-rank manifold.
RoM obtains the highest mean accuracy on both downstream benchmarks for the Llama models, although the differences are small relative to variation across seeds.

selections.summary: Uses Nyström sketches and quantized optimizer states for LLM pretraining. For LLaMA-1.3B, Table 3 reports Q-Clean optimizer-state memory of 1.28G and peak memory of 50.24G, versus Muon’s 2.80G and 51.83G; Q-Clean’s perplexity is 12.10 versus Muon’s 11.78.
